/legal/terms-of-service.title: Terms of Service — Diffusion
/legal/terms-of-service.description: What Diffusion stores about a reader — a name and an email address, nothing else — and the terms of using the site.
h6: Diffusion is a free, public, open-source dashboard run by one person. There is nothing to buy and nothing to subscribe to, so these terms are mostly a description of what the site is rather than a contract you are being held to.
p: Read it, quote it, disagree with it in public. No permission needed.
Do not attack the server or try to reach other readers' accounts. There is nothing in them, but still.
There is no password to keep confidential.
A real name and a real address are appreciated. Neither is checked.
This is one person's project, and it may change or stop:
Nothing here costs money, and no part of it is held back for a paid tier.
An account used to attack the site will be removed.
The economic data on this site belongs to the statistical agencies that publish it, not to Diffusion. Each source carries its own licence, and that licence is shown on every series page.
Cite and link the publisher. For anything that matters, take the numbers from them rather than from here.
The code is MIT licensed and on GitHub. Do what you like with it.
The written analysis is its author's. The page design is adapted from a commercial template under that template's own licence.
The institutional reports cited in the literature sections belong to their publishers. They are linked and quoted, never redistributed.
There is no subscription, no paid tier and no trial.
No card is asked for and no payment is processed anywhere on this site.
If that ever changes it will be said plainly and in advance, not by quietly editing this page.
Diffusion is provided as is, with no warranty.
Data is ingested from public sources automatically and can be wrong, stale or misattributed. Where a page knows its evidence is weak, it says so on the page.
Nothing here is investment, financial or policy advice. It is a reading of published statistics.
These may change. The version and date at the top say when they last did.
Nothing is being agreed to that costs you anything.

/legal/privacy-policy.title: Privacy Policy — Diffusion
/legal/privacy-policy.description: What Diffusion stores about a reader — a name and an email address, nothing else — and the terms of using the site.
h6: Diffusion is run by one person and holds two pieces of information about you: a name and an email address, typed into a sign-in form. This page says what happens to them. It is short because very little happens to them.
p: This is the complete list, not a summary of it:
The name and the email address you type into the sign-in form.
Nothing else. No analytics, no tracking pixels, no advertising identifiers, no third-party scripts.
No record of what you read, no device fingerprint, and no IP address log kept against your account.
Anything you choose to send me, which is read by one person.
The address is used for exactly one thing, and here is the honest version of it:
To know roughly who the work reaches. That is the entire reason an account exists.
To reply, if you write in with a correction.
You will not be emailed otherwise. There is no mailing list, no newsletter and no product announcement.
The address is never verified, so it is a visitor record rather than a credential, and it protects nothing.
Nothing behind the sign-in is private — it is public statistics from public sources — so there is nothing here for an account to guard.
The row is stored in a Postgres database and read by nobody but the person who runs the site.
Nothing is sold, rented, traded or shared. Not in aggregate either.
Nothing is inferred, scored, enriched or joined against any other source.
Nobody. Named individually, so this cannot be read generously:
The database host stores the row, because it stores every row. There is no analytics provider, because there are no analytics.
A lawful order would be complied with. There would be very little to hand over.

No external service is loaded by any page here. The typefaces are served from this site rather than from Google Fonts, which is a change from an earlier version of this policy: nothing about your visit reaches a third party.

No password is set, sent, hashed or stored by either sign-in route, so there is nothing here that could be stolen and replayed against another site. A session is a signed cookie rather than a stored token. What is held is a name and an unverified email address, and no system can promise perfect security of even that.
Wherever you are, and without having to cite a regulation:
Ask what is stored under your address, or ask for it to be deleted, using the contact link at the end of this page. It will be, and you will get a reply saying so.
There is no processing to restrict, and the portable version of your record is a name and an email address.
Signing out and not coming back also works.

/.title: Diffusion — Is AI changing the economy?
/.description: Artificial intelligence's measurable effect on the world economy, read through five lenses and built only from official statistics. Every number links back to the agency that published it.
h2: Read the argument, then check the data
The rules are the point. Everything else is implementation
Technology diffusion, where anyone has measured it
What this is, and what it is not
h3: From a named source to a stated finding
Five lenses, in the order the causation is supposed to run
What other people have found, and where they disagree
Disagreement needs a scope check, not a vote
p: Named sources · Dated evidence · Stated limits
Each question shows the claim being tested, how this page measures it, and where it fails.

Statistical agencies, public data services and research publishers supply the evidence. Series link to their sources and state their licences; the source register separates working feeds from unverified or unavailable connections.
Not just the answer. The mechanism being claimed, the measurement used, and the confound that would break it.
Every claim sits directly above the series it rests on. Follow it in either direction.
These series say not yet. But several studies measuring at a finer grain say otherwise, and the likeliest reconciliation is that this page is asking at the wrong resolution.
What this does not show: a national youth unemployment rate averages away an effect concentrated in a few exposed occupations.
Every figure links to its source
Evidence and review status shown on each question
Money is spent, output does or does not rise, jobs change, prices move, governments respond.
What is being spent, and what it buys
Whether any of it shows up in output
Jobs and pay, what it costs, and what governments are doing
Illustration using the 3 September 2026 database snapshot, not live coverage. Open the app for current scope.
The 2026 AI Index Report — Economy chapter
Is the exposed sector shrinking? — contested
Headcount cuts attributed to AI: observed against expected, by business function, 2025
Not yet checked by a person
Institutional and consulting reports, cited and linked. Claims are distinguished from extracted figures, with evidence scope and review status shown. A publisher name is not a quality guarantee.
Figures are quoted and linked back to the report. Nothing is rehosted.
Labelled by kind, not by rank
A consultancy survey and a central bank paper are both shown, and named as what they are.
Marked where it disagrees with us
A source that contradicts the page it sits on stays on that page, saying so.
Results can differ because populations, outcomes, methods and periods differ. The source scope is checked before treating findings as contradictions.
Consistent, suggestive, insufficient or contested, printed beside the answer.
When the series cannot separate the answers, the page says so instead of picking one.
Contested is stated, not smoothed over
Unlike outcomes and populations are not averaged into a single economic effect.
For AI and employment, PwC and IMF results cover different populations and outcomes, so they are presented separately, not as opposing estimates of one effect.
Four constraints this site holds itself to, whether or not anyone checks
Series calculations and machine-assisted report extractions have different provenance. Review states and source locators show what has actually been checked.
Stated under the answer and above every chart.
Charts are not allowed to flatter
One y-axis. Zero baseline. Gaps break the line.
Enterprise AI-use survey examples. Populations and reference periods differ; these are not a global adoption ranking.
How the data is gathered, how the claims are made, and where both fall short.
Where does the data come from?

From named public sources including FRED, the World Bank, Census, DBnomics and SEC EDGAR, alongside research publishers. Series link to their sources and state their licences. The source register shows what is implemented, verified and current; a configured connection alone is not evidence of coverage.

A scheduled ingestion workflow checks available sources; successful runs and reference dates are shown separately. Data can lag its publication schedule. Numerical summaries are reconstructed from current facts, while research and editorial claims have separate review states.
Is any of this written by AI?

AI assists research and drafting. Numerical summaries use validated data facts rather than unconstrained generated numbers. Research claims and report extractions carry evidence and review states; machine extraction or a citation alone is not proof that a claim has been verified.

That evidence supports competing interpretations. Different populations, methods or time periods may explain a disagreement; results are not treated as direct contradictions until their scope is checked. The unresolved question and limitations remain visible.
Take it from the publisher, on their terms — each one's licence is shown on its series page. The code is MIT and the whole project is open source.

Coverage is uneven by country and question. Broad macroeconomic series are not direct evidence of AI adoption or impact. Comparable adoption surveys, occupation-level outcomes and causal identification remain limited. Country pages show usable series, reference dates and source-specific gaps rather than treating every country as equally measured.
If you are an economist and a comparison here is unsound, that is the most useful thing you could tell me.
